#852. From sketch to publication-ready flowchart: how AI tools can bridge the gap

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Ensar Aydemir is an endocrinologist at Sultan 1. Murat State Hospital in Edirne, Türkiye. X: @dreaydemir

Artificial-intelligence tools can speed up the process of generating publication-ready flowcharts. Credit: -MG-/Getty

When making a scientific diagram, whether I am outlining a clinical study, planning a flowchart or mapping a signalling pathway, I often start in the same way: with a pen and a piece of paper.

Sketching by hand is fast. I can draw a box, cross something out and reorganize a whole idea without thinking about fonts, alignment or software menus. At this stage, my aim is not to make the figure beautiful, it is to work out the logic.

Turning that rough sketch into a clean figure for a manuscript can be surprisingly tedious, however. Text boxes need to line up; arrows need to connect properly; and fonts, spacing and colours must be consistent. A diagram that took five minutes to draw might take an hour or longer to recreate digitally.

Multimodal artificial-intelligence tools can shorten this process. Rather than asking an AI model to create the final scientific image, I use it as a translator. The model reads my sketch, interprets its structure and converts it into editable diagram code that I can open in a vector-based editor, such as Draw.io — a free application for making diagrams.

This distinction matters. I do not want AI to invent a figure for me; I want it to help me to digitize a figure that I have already designed.

One tempting approach is to provide a description to an image-generation model and ask for a polished scientific figure.

For research diagrams, this can create more problems than it solves. Text might be misspelt, arrows misdirected and pathways altered. More importantly, the resulting image is usually flat (that is, the text, images and background are merged together), making it mostly uneditable. For diagrams in research publications, if a reviewer later asks you to alter it, you might have to start from scratch.

A better option is to ask a multimodal language model — for example, Google’s Gemini — to turn your idea into a structured diagram format, such as Draw.io-compatible XML or Mermaid syntax. The output can then be imported into a diagram editor, in which every box, label and connector remains editable.

In this workflow, AI is less an illustrator than a compiler: a programming tool that translates human-readable instructions into code that a computer can run. My sketch is the source, and Draw.io XML is the output.

Focus first on the structure of your figure. I roughly sketch the important nodes, branches and connections without worrying about visual polish. For a clinical study, these might include eligibility criteria, treatment groups and follow-up visits. For a laboratory workflow, they might represent experimental stages or decision points.

The key is to make the relationships clear. What box comes first? Where does the pathway split? Which arrow connects to which endpoint? If the logic is ambiguous to a human reader, it will be ambiguous to the AI model, too.

Once the sketch is complete, I photograph it, upload the image to a vision-enabled language model and provide a detailed prompt. For instance:

“Recreate the uploaded hand-drawn figure as a clean, editable academic flowchart in Draw.io-compatible XML format. Preserve the original structure as faithfully as possible, including box positions, arrows, dashed connectors, side boxes, branching pattern, and text content. This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task. Use a plain white background, thin dark slate-grey borders, white box fills, thin connector lines, clean sans-serif text, and no shadows, gradients, or decorative elements. Make it publication-quality while keeping it recognizably the same diagram.”

The instruction “This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task” is crucial. Scientific diagrams are not the place for creative completion. I want the model to reconstruct my structure, not improve it on my behalf.

Note also that this prompt indicates what the model should not change. I explicitly ask it to preserve wording, branching relationships and directionality. If the diagram contains important numbers, doses or time points, I check each one manually.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03513-1

#851. Liverpool v Man Utd referee made ‘obvious error’ sending off Leny Yoro as written reasons published

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Man Utd defender’s suspension has been overturned, with an independent regulatory commission unanimously concluding that Referee Sam Barrott’s decision was wrong

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Referee Sam Barrott made an “obvious error” by giving Manchester United defender Leny Yoro a red card against Liverpool, an independent regulatory commission unanimously concluded.

Yoro was given his marching orders when he hauled down Swedish striker Alexander Isak in the opening stages of last Sunday’s fiery match at Anfield.

Debate raged over Isak’s touch and whether goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have collected the ball had Yoro not made contact.

Even referees’ chief Howard Webb concluded that the call was “certainly not clearly wrong”, but then Manchester United appealed to the Football Association for wrongful dismissal and successfully removed his one-match ban on Tuesday.

The three-person panel’s written reasons were published on Thursday and stated: “The commission members were unanimous that, taking the foul committed by LY (Yoro) out of the scenario, AI (Isak) would not have had an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

“Despite the fact that AI had reached the ball initially, his touch was heavy to the extent that he had in fact lost control of the ball – that control had, in effect, passed to the advancing MUFC goalkeeper who in the view of the commission would have been able to gather or smother the ball before AI could get to it and shoot at goal.

“To the mind of the commission, the referee had made an ‘obvious error’ in deciding that AI (Isak) would have had an obvious goalscoring opportunity.”

Webb, the chief refereeing officer at Pro Ref, told the Match Officials: Mic’d Up programme which aired on Tuesday, shortly after confirmation the ban had been removed: “There’s a question mark I guess around whether or not he (Isak) would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

“The VAR checks to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn’t.

“I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it’s a little bit debatable. (It’s) certainly not clearly wrong.”

The FA’s independent panel, which was made up of former Blackburn and Middlesbrough winger Stuart Ripley, former Sheffield United and Notts County forward Tony Agana and ex-Walsall goalkeeper Mick Kearns, disagreed.

The reasons confirm that United submitted technical information to the panel which concluded Isak would have been, at best, 1.8 metres short of the ball even if Yoro had not made the challenge.

The reasons state that the commission “had no way of testing the validity of this analysis undertaken by the club and as such the evidence was viewed with caution and allocated weight accordingly”.

To add to the confusion, the Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel is reported by the Daily Mail to have backed Barrott’s call and the decision of the VAR John Brooks not to recommend a review.

The five-person KMI Panel is comprised of three former players and coaches, one Premier League representative and one from Pro Ref, and its findings for the match week where the incident occurred are due to be published on December 2.

Pro Ref declined to comment on the Mail story, or on the commission’s findings. Manchester United have been approached for comment.

The reasons revealed that United also submitted a video of a challenge by Brighton’s Pascal Struijk on Wilson Isidor of Sunderland last month. Struijk was shown a red card after the VAR recommended a review for denial of an obvious goalscoring opportunity. Struijk’s suspension was removed after an appeal to the FA by Brighton.

The removal of the ban means Yoro is free to face Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday.

United encountered further refereeing controversy in their 2-2 Champions League draw away to Sporting in Lisbon on Wednesday night.

The Red Devils had a first-half goal disallowed after Polish referee Szymon Marciniak blew for what looked at best a very soft-looking foul by Youri Tielemans before Amad Diallo had put the ball in the net. They then had a winner ruled out when VAR recommended a review for what was deemed to be a foul by United’s Patrick Dorgu on Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira, though the Brazilian appeared to have fumbled into his own net before the Dorgu challenge came in.

To rub salt into their wounds, Tielemans – who was booked for the challenge that led to the Diallo goal being disallowed – was then shown a second yellow in injury time.

The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.

"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he said.

"An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done."

The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.

Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.

Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway, a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.

In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.

The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

The long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.

#844. The Spygate reunion that proves Southampton and Tonda Eckert got off lightly

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Southampton face Middlesbrough for the first time since the ‘Spygate’ scandal - but with Tonda Eckert still in a job and Saints flying high, Will Castle questions whether justice was really done

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

When Southampton were kicked out of the Championship play-off final four days before football’s richest game, there was a bubbling dread that things were about to spiral.

‘Spygate’ had rocked English football to its core. It started with an intern, camera in hand, failing to adequately hide behind a tree outside Middlesbrough’s training ground, birthing the cartoonish image that will forever be the thumbnail of this scandal. What subsequently unravelled was far more sinister; a pattern of cheating by Saints that was driven by those at the very top. As the club was put under the spotlight, they also admitted to espionage against Ipswich and Oxford before being caught red-handed spying on their play-off semi-final opponents.

Tonda Eckert wasn’t simply complicit in sending staff out to spy on rivals; he spearheaded the plot. Findings of the League Arbitration Panel investigating the scandal laid bare of the Saints boss’ influence in “a contrived and determined plan from top down to gain a competitive advantage”, which left junior staff feeling “compelled to do what they were very uncomfortable doing because they considered their jobs would otherwise be at risk”.

“Deplorable” was the word used to describe this scheme, and it resulted in an unprecedented punishment. Saints were expelled from the play-off final and stripped of their shot at promotion back to the Premier League, along with the £200m in riches that come with it. They were also handed a four-point deduction for the start of the 2026/27 Championship season. The club called this "manifestly disproportionate to every previous sanction in the history of the English game". But it felt like this was only the start.

Eckert, who at just 33 had been building a reputation as one of English football’s most promising young managers, was at serious risk of seeing his rise completely derailed. The FA swiftly opened an investigation into the German and a lengthy ban from football was on the table for bringing the game into disrepute. Had he been slapped with a months-long suspension, Southampton - who wanted to stand by their manager - would have been forced into unwanted turmoil in the dugout.

Instead, Eckert - who took responsibility and admitted the misconduct charges - escaped serious punishment. He was given a six-week suspended ban and a £28,000 fine.

Now, two months on from this verdict and six months since ‘Spygate’ erupted, Eckert will lead his side into their first post-scandal meeting with Middlesbrough. He’ll do so having just signed a new contract.

There is a fair argument to say Eckert, as an individual responsible for his own behaviour, got off lightly. In any other job, such an abuse of power would usually result in the sack. Southampton chose to back him, which is their prerogative - Eckert has the best win rate of any Saints manager since the 1890s, so it’s no surprise they wanted to avoid losing the German. But both club and manager are fortunate that the FA opted against a full measure, which would have effectively taken his future out of their hands.

Still at the helm, Eckert has been empowered to oversee a recovery at St Mary’s, to the point where the shockwaves of ‘Spygate’ are no longer really being felt. The four-point deduction was swiftly made up at the start of the season and the club are now seven points off the top and very much in the promotion hunt. Their formidable home form sets them apart, unbeaten in 18 on their own turf.

Tipped for a season of chaos in the summer, they welcome league leaders Boro almost back on their perch by November. The visitors might feel a tinge of injustice at just how quickly they’ve managed to return to this point, especially with Eckert still pulling the strings.

Eckert hinted that hostilities between him and Boro boss Kim Hellberg had been quelled in his pre-match press conference on Thursday. The Swede said he had sleepless nights due to the “disgraceful” actions of his opposition, but Eckert stated the pair spoke on the phone earlier this year and that both will go into Friday’s clash with only the end result in mind. "We've had a conversation on the phone and we saw each other at the EFL day before the season,” he said. “We are two managers who will try to win a game and that's it."

Boro are out for redemption this term. Their last-minute ticket to the play-off final went in vain when hearts were broken by Ollie McBurnie at Wembley. They look well-placed to go one better this season, though, fuelled by a fantastic summer transfer window which saw them bring in, among others, the league’s current top scorer Will Lankshear from Tottenham.

But for all their sins, Saints still harbour the feeling that they emerged from this scandal wronged by their sanction; akin to a poor man’s Weimar Germany after World War One. Before Eckert learned his fate at the hands of the FA, chief executive Phil Parsons claimed the club had “taken enough” punishment, chiefly their play-off expulsion. He complained about the legal fees and the money being lost by local businesses, almost as if to drive pity for the club. And while he stated: “We don’t want to be seen as a victim of this,” that is the narrative that is held in parts of Southampton.

Ultimately, however, Saints were let off the hook to the extent where the club could keep Eckert and rejuvenate before the New Year. Any victim sentiment is borderline deluded, and that’s evidenced by the state of play going into a ‘Spygate’ reunion. This is a promotion six-pointer; Southampton should count themselves lucky to be in such a promising position.

#843. SFA to deliver revised proposal after young player vote delayed

The Scottish FA will continue to consult with SPFL clubs about youth development after initial plans failed to reach a member vote.

At a summit in September, Scottish football's governing body proposed financial incentives and penalties along with quotas, in a bid to get more homegrown talent playing for Scottish clubs.

Initially, the plans were to have been voted on at an SFA general meeting in October and the SPFL's annual meeting this month.

But the SFA are now aiming to put refreshed proposals to the clubs early in the new year, with the plan to implement them for the start of the 2027-28 season.

Despite being "encouraged", the governing body added that "recent discussions have spawned a range of additional potential innovations that all parties agree will require further consultation."

"The passion we all have for Scottish football has been demonstrated by the public debate sparked since the all-club meeting in St Andrews," a Scottish FA statement read.

"We will continue to engage in dialogue with the aim of delivering a proposal that will achieve the stated objective of improving opportunities for young homegrown players to fulfil their potential at the top end of the Scottish professional game."

"It is an objective everyone benefits from: players, clubs, supporters and Scotland national teams."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

At their initial consultation with clubs, the SFA put forward three proposals:

Two under-21 Scotland-eligible players start in all Scottish Cup matches, with one player on the pitch at all times.

Two under-21 Scotland-eligible players start in all Premier Sports Cup matches, with one player on the pitch at all times.

Clubs should field Scotland-eligible Under-21 players for an average of 60 minutes in each game across all four SPFL divisions

Xabi Alonso says Wesley Fofana has apologised to Chelsea after giving an explosive interview without the club’s permission.

A two-hour conversation with Fofana was published by French YouTuber Zach Nani on Friday, during which the 25-year-old appeared to joke about missing a penalty in Chelsea’s shootout defeat to Liverpool which knocked them out of the Carabao Cup.

Asked whether Fofana would face any further sanction, such as be dropped from the squad, or if the case was closed, Alonso replied: “Closed.”

Ethan Nwaneri's Arsenal career appears to be floundering, with the on-loan Borussia Dortmund teenager facing a further transfer setback.

Nwaneri returns to his parent club tonight in the Champions League with the Bundesliga giants and is eligible to face Arsenal despite still being owned by the Gunners.

But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.

Nwaneri became the Premier League's youngest-ever player in 2022 at the age of 15 – with Max Dowman later taking that record – before establishing himself in the 2024/25 season as a serious option on the right wing for the Gunners.

But after going out on loan at Marseille last term and heading to Dortmund this time, the teenager is yet to impress, with Arteta even admitting this week that “moments are not enough” for Nwaneri in his development and that consistency must follow.

FourFourTwo understands that the Gunners were open to offers for the starlet over the summer, opting to retain him and develop him at one of the best finishing schools in European football, though the paths of Nwaneri and Hale End colleague Myles Lewis-Skelly have been drastically different, thanks, in part, due to competition for places.

A clip of Jude Bellingham standing up for a female reporter who was interrupted during a post-match interview has gone viral.

#839. Hemmings unfazed by rise at Villa and eager to take next step

Sky Sports sits down with Aston Villa prospect George Hemmings to discuss his rise to the first team; Hemmings started for seven games before an injury curtailed progress; watch Ipswich vs Aston Villa live on Saturday Night Football, kick-off 5.30pm

Football Journalist @PatrickRoweSky

Two days after being thrown into a cauldron in Istanbul during Aston Villa's loss to Galatasaray in the Champions League, George Hemmings strolls into the media centre at Bodymoor Heath, sliders on, looking entirely at home in the senior surroundings that should be new to him.

The nineteen-year-old is quiet and reserved to start but soon settled into proceedings when quizzed on that atmosphere and what the experience was like.

"It was mad," he says with a smile on his face. "When we had the ball, you couldn't hear anything but whistling."

The mentality to take to an occasion such as that is largely expected by prospects in the modern game. A lofty standard set by the likes of Max Dowman and Rio Ngumoha.

But it does not mean we should lose sight of it.

For comparison, the journalist typing this was pulling on the ASDA shirt at the same age.

Hemmings, meanwhile, has been fast-tracked into the senior squad at Villa, thrust into an industry where the scrutiny and pressure is unmatched, and has impressed in the early stages of his career.

Unai Emery has an eye for talent and a knack for helping prospects tap into their potential. He wouldn't provide the platform for Hemmings if he didn't see something in the versatile midfielder.

"He is really good with me. He is always just looking for the best and always trying to improve me," he says when asked about the guidance Emery offers.

A quick glance out the window and you can see his team-mate, Taylor Harwood-Bellis, leaving. But it is two chairs and a spotlight for Hemmings, rather than an early exit.

His answers are short and snappy. A young prospect still getting to grips with the added responsibilities that come with being a Premier League footballer. But just like on the pitch, he takes it in his stride.

I move the conversation onto his quick rise into the first team. Following a summer of change at Villa Park, where Morgan Rogers, Ollie Watkins, Youri Tielemans, Ezri Konsa and more all departed, Hemmings was a shock inclusion in the starting line-up against Brighton on the opening day of the season.

A chastening 4-0 defeat would follow at the Amex Stadium, but in the brief spells of positive play from 10-man Villa on that day, Hemmings showed the flashes of talent that have caught the eye of Emery since day one.

He went on to start all seven games to begin 2026/27 before a knee injury curtailed his progress, with a first goal for the senior side still eluding him. He is yet to start a game since returning but Villa have reaffirmed their belief in the player after he penned a new five-year deal at the club.

"I am excited! It is five years, so I have a long time to improve myself and improve my game." I then pose the question of where he may see himself in his career in five years' time, where he adds: "We will have to see! I just have to keep working."

It is clear he is firmly in the plans of Emery and also revealed conversations about a potential loan exit before the season began never occurred.

"I always look at what is best for my career and once I saw that I could get a few games, I was always going to stay," he continued.

The 2-1 win against Coventry, arguably his strongest performance in a Villa shirt so far, offered a glimpse into what Emery is trying to coerce out of the young talent.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tammy Abraham's opener at the CBS Arena came courtesy of a moment of real quality from Hemmings. His perfectly placed pass with the outside of his right boot dissected Premier League opposition and made the finish easy for his team-mate.

It offered an insight into the quality Villa hope he can one day produce regularly. But the celebrations also outlined why he is in the perfect environment for that necessary development.

Abraham quickly pointed to Hemmings and embraced his team-mate. Captain John McGinn arrived with a tap on the head, with Ross Barkley and Ibrahim Mbaye following suit.

The next opportunity to impress arrives on Saturday as Villa face Ipswich, live on Sky Sports, with a six-game winless run looming over the squad.

Hemmings was already around the squad prior to the major changes that occurred over the summer. Should he continue his current trajectory, he could become an increasingly important part of Emery's plans for years to come.

At 19, he still has plenty to learn but if his early steps in senior football are anything to go by, he is unlikely to be overawed by whatever the game can throw at him. It was a short encounter with Hemmings - but you can see why he is rated so highly at the club.

#838. Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

The US is now officially a measles contagion zone. By mid-2026, there were more infections than in all of the previous year. But the country could beat measles again, just like Brazil did two years ago.

Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:

It has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.

In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Data from Europe shows that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

Measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

#835. Germany star ruled out of Women’s World Cup 2027 after accepting doping ban

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Laura Freigang has been suspended after three whereabouts failures

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Germany forward Laura Freigang will miss next summer’s Women’s World Cup after accepting a suspension over failure to comply with doping regulations.

The Eintracht Frankfurt captain was accused of failing to provide a drugs test or submit her whereabouts for testing on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026, thereby breaching the World Anti-Doping Code.

She reached an settlement agreement with WADA, Germany’s National Anti-Doping Agency, and the German football federation over the case, which has resulted in a 16-month ban backdated to 8 June 2026, the day she was notified of the case against her.

It means she will not be eligible to return to football until 8 October 2027. She will miss the Women’s World Cup, which runs from 24 June to 25 July, in Brazil.

The 28-year-old can return to training two months before the expiry of the ban.

Eintracht Frankfurt announced the news on Thursday, with the club to “soon begin discussions to establish the structuring of their future contract [with Freigang] in light of this suspension”. Freigang’s contract runs until 30 June next year.

Freigang released a statement on Instagram saying: “It is important for me to emphasise once again that at no time was there any suspicion of doping against me.

“The last few months have been extremely hard for me. Further proceedings would have meant high financial, mental and emotional burdens for me. That's why I chose this way, in the hope of finding some calm, clarity and perspective for myself.”

She added: “It breaks my heart not to be able to be on the field, helping my team and being able to live the everyday life that I love so much.”

None of Eintracht Frankfurt’s results since her ban began in June are affected.

Katharina Kiel, director of women’s football, said: “The agreement that has now been reached provides clarity and planning certainty in a process that is unique to Eintracht Frankfurt – for us as a club, but above all for Laura.

“The way she and the team have handled the situation over the past few months, and the way Laura personally led by example on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the utmost recognition.

“At Eintracht Frankfurt, we have witnessed the strong sense of unity that characterises this club. We will calmly discuss the future and the details of our working relationship with Laura.”

Freigang has 45 caps for Germany and was a member of the squad which reached the Euro 2022 final. She has been at Eintracht Frankfurt since 2018.

#834. Can Beijing scale up its smart-city ambitions?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hepeng Jia is a freelance science writer based in Suzhou, China.

Yizhuang, the district of Beijing where this Lingyi iTech robotics factory is located, is a key area of the city for demonstrating leading smart-city solutions.Credit: Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images

In Yizhuang, a high-tech industrial zone in Beijing, drivers have access to parts of roads, highways and intersections where they might experience green lights all the way. Networks of road cameras and sensors feed data to a local control centre, which issues app notifications to drivers about upcoming interruptions, recommended driving speeds and lane suggestions to keep the traffic moving. On these ‘green-wave corridors’, the average number of traffic stops throughout the day has dropped by 40.6%, and the average travel speed has increased by 15.1%, according to local reports.

Also known as the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, or Beijing E-Town, Yizhuang was created in the early 1990s by the Beijing Municipal People’s Government to act as the city’s leading smart-city demonstration zone. Alongside its intelligent transport systems, it has become a key area for autonomous-vehicle development and robotics, often showcasing emerging technologies at public events.

The annual Beijing E-Town Half-Marathon, for example, attracts hundreds of humanoid robots built by companies and university teams to compete with humans over an almost 22-kilometre track. In 2025, the inaugural year of the race, many robots failed to finish. But in this year’s race, held in April, the robots showed major improvements in speed, reliability and autonomy.

Alongside Yizhuang, Beijing has many other smart-city ‘brains’ — hubs of innovation that are fast-tracking technological development in strategic areas such as artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and data governance.

One such area is Haidian in northwest Beijing, which runs a spatial-mapping platform that functions as a digital twin of the district. Gathering data from some 170,000 buildings, plus tens of thousands of road cameras and sensors, the platform flags local faults and automatically generates work orders to speed up repairs. The repair-response time for missing manhole covers, for instance, which is a major hazard for drivers and pedestrians, has been reduced from a whole day to just four hours. Haidian is home to Peking University and Tsinghua University — two of China’s leading academic institutions in the Nature Index — as well as the country’s greatest concentration of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) institutes.

Underpinning Beijing’s smart-city ambitions is its enormous investment in science and technology. Beijing has been the leading science city in the Nature Index since 2016, and in 2025, its Share in the natural and health sciences was about two-thirds higher than that of its closest competitor, Shanghai. That year, Beijing spent around 6% of its gross domestic product on R&D — the highest share in the country. The city’s sprawling research system has formed close ties with its private AI sector, which, as of 2024, encompassed about 2,400 companies worth nearly 350 billion yuan (US$51.7 billion).

A key challenge for Beijing is how to link all of the data being collected by its various districts and zones. Different departments might not feel incentivized to share their data or link up with central databases, says Yuan Zhibin, a senior research fellow at the CAS Institute of Science and Technology Strategy Consulting in Beijing. Strong competition between Beijing’s leading technology districts, such as Yizhuang and Haidian, as well as the costs involved in changing or updating systems, are major factors, says Yuan.

#833. Russell: I found Verstappen comments amusing

George Russell's long-standing feud with Max Verstappen reignited at the Las Vegas GP after the pair collided in final practice; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

George Russell says he was "amused" by Max Verstappen’s criticism of him after their feud reignited at the Las Vegas Grand Prix but admits it was "avoidable".

After colliding on track in final practice last weekend, Russell publicly criticised Verstappen following the incident. The Dutchman won the race after an intense battle between them and said afterwards that the Mercedes driver is "far below my level".

The pair have clashed several times on track in the past, most notably engaging in a remarkable war of words following an incident during qualifying at the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had pushed unreasonably hard for him to be penalised.

Speaking on Thursday - back at the Lusail International Circuit almost exactly two years on from that incident - ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, Russell said: "At the end of the day, I guess I stand by what I said after practice.

"But he was the one who went out and won the race. I didn't and I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about that, and that was reasonably amusing. From my side, just a new race weekend, try and focus on the driving and move on."

Russell was pressed on the saga throughout the FIA press conference and revealed he was perhaps "guilty of being just too open and honest when I speak with you guys [the media]".

"It's all avoidable at the end of the day, and it's all a bit unnecessary. It's not something I'm looking to continue. I'm not looking to have poor relationships with people. That's just not really the type of person I am," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"There are lessons just to be taken away from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media because I feel that I'm having more of an open conversation with you guys as opposed to remembering there's a camera.

"There are more people in this room than there are cameras, and I feel like I'm talking to you, but I'm not actually talking to you. I need to remind myself that I'm talking to the camera there that's broadcasting to millions of people. That's the biggest takeaway."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Verstappen did not want to make any further comments about his Russell feud during his media sessions at the Lusail International Circuit.

"Everything else that has been said off track has been said. There's nothing else to add," he said.

Russell had been battling with Verstappen for the lead during most of the Las Vegas Grand Prix as a combination of a big slipstream effect and the new 2026 power units created a peloton-style race.

However, the Mercedes driver was third with three laps to go behind Verstappen and team-mate Kimi Antonelli, so went for a move on the latter at Turn 5 but crashed and eventually finished ninth.

Verstappen, who is likely to finish second in the Drivers' Championship this season, said it was "fantastic" when he saw Russell in the wall.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Russell said: "I don't think it's important to have a good relationship or no relationship in that regard to be honest. We're all fighting for race wins. My mistake in Vegas came when I was trying to overtake my team-mate.

"The truth is, my risk dial is probably a bit too great at the moment, because I'm just kind of wanting to go for these big results and get some highlights on the board towards the end of the season.

"If that was race one of the season, there's no way I would have gone for that move with two laps remaining. But two races to go in the season, I kind of wanted to go for it.

"I think the majority of us respect one another out there, and we have hard and good battles. and even the race with Max until that point was good and fair. It was very strategic."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Russell reiterated that he respects Verstappen "immensely for his driving talent and everything he's achieved on track" and feels he does not have to be friends with the four-time world champion.

"At the end of the day, we're all competitors out there. I think there's no right or wrong way about the mentality that everybody has, and I think we're all different in many regards, and you don't need to agree with one another," he said.

"I'm not looking to be best mates with anybody on the grid. I'm just working and looking and fighting to win. Simple as that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

McLaren's Lando Norris, who has fought Verstappen on track several times in recent years, agrees with Russell.

"You don't have to get on. Do you get on with everyone?" he said.

"It's just normal. It happens in life; not everyone agrees with everything. It's also a sport where you want to prove that you're better than everyone else.

"You can either do your talking on the track or you can do your talking in front of a camera. It normally always helps when you can back it up on track, that's what everyone, at the end of the day, really cares about, but I still respect both drivers a lot.

"Obviously, Max has proved to everyone [what] he's capable of and George is kind of still I think yet to prove what he's capable of. I still think he can achieve a lot in his Formula 1 career and look forward to seeing that. He's obviously had a tough year but I still believe he can have a good season and I look forward to more times when he's giving a good fight to Max."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Verstappen's former Red Bull team-mate Pierre Gasly half-joked he is "sitting and eating my popcorn and laughing" about the Verstappen-Russell spat.

"I think it was best with Max just to tell him right up in his face! He's someone that just takes anything," said the Alpine driver.

"You can have opinions, etcetera. I like both of them, obviously [they are] very different. We all know each other, we know each other since we were kids. It's not the first time, it's not the last time, these two are going to go at it."

Are the Premier League’s London clubs at an advantage? Arsenal prepare to put that unique theory to the test

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Having made their longest Premier League away trip of the season to Newcastle last week, Arsenal can settle into familiar surroundings for the festive period: the Gunners don’t leave London again until mid-January when they travel to Hull.

Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

That’s the third of 11 straight games in the capital for the Gunners, which will become 12 if they’re drawn at home in the third round of the FA Cup, beginning with Tuesday’s Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund. Recent history suggests an interesting theory about such home comforts.

Eleven games into their title defence, Arsenal sit second in the Premier League away table with four wins, one draw and one defeat from six games on the road. Not that it’s anything new for the Gunners to occupy such heights: they’ve boasted the top flight’s best away record in each of the last four seasons.

And that comes with the territory of being a London club. Across the last 10 Premier League campaigns not impacted by pandemic crowd restrictions (so excluding 2019/20 and 2020/21), only once have more clubs from London had a bottom-half away record than a top-half away record. That was last term, when four of the seven London clubs finished in the bottom 10 of the away table (Crystal Palace, Brentford, Fulham and West Ham).

In each of the other nine seasons in question, at least 57 per cent of the Premier League’s London clubs have finished with one of the best 10 away records in the division; in 2016/17, all five of them did (Chelsea, Tottenham, Arsenal, Palace and West Ham).

So, is it an advantage to be a London club?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There’s not really a simple answer to that question (sorry), but we can still pull together some interesting takeaways.

This season, the average Premier League club will travel 153 kilometres for an away fixture. For two clubs, that average climbs to over 300km: the league’s two most north-easterly sides, Sunderland (350km) and Newcastle (347km), and the most south-westerly, Bournemouth (317km). Conversely, one side will travel a touch under 200km on average: Coventry (198km) – in that sense, you might consider the Sky Blues the ultimate Midlands club.

But the top-flight’s six London clubs all sit in the bottom eight of the league in terms of average away travel distance, with Palace travelling the furthest (227km) and Spurs the least far (202km). And the very fact that those sides account for just over a quarter of the division means short trips are a regular occurrence.

And for Arsenal, this 11-match stretch that sees them go no further than Brentford could not fall at a better time than the notoriously hectic festive period – certainly when it comes to maximising recovery time between fixtures, which come thick and fast an average of one game every 4.2 days between now and January 5 (though it’s worth noting that turnaround is still below the UEFA-recommended minimum window of five days between matches).

Could the timing of Arsenal’s London residency, so to speak, prove crucial to another successful Premier League title push? Well, they’re already six points clear at the top and look like they could walk it, given Manchester City’s dramatic recent drop-off, but minimising time spent on the road during one of the busiest stages of the campaign seems unlikely to work to their detriment.

That being said, a quick word on Chelsea: the Blues have left London three times all season but are languishing in mid-table in the Premier League and are out of the Carabao Cup. So, maybe there’s something to be said for getting out of town on a more regular basis. Besides, it’s not like elite-level players these days are travelling in anything less than luxury, is it?

Tom Hancock started freelancing for FourFourTwo in April 2019 and has also written for the Premier League and Opta Analyst, among others. He supports Wycombe Wanderers and has a soft spot for Wealdstone. A self-confessed statto, he has been known to watch football with a spreadsheet (or several) open...

#831. PL Predictions: How will your club fare this weekend?

Watch Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea, Ipswich vs Aston Villa, Crystal Palace vs Hull, Brighton vs Newcastle, Fulham vs Bournemouth, Sunderland vs Tottenham and Arsenal vs Manchester City all live on Sky Sports; play Super 6 on SUNDAY to win £1m!

Our top tipster Lewis Jones, aka Jones Knows, provides his analysis and betting insight across the Premier League.

I'm not for jumping off the Nottingham Forest bandwagon just yet.

Forest have taken just four points from their last seven Premier League games - no team has taken fewer - yet they sit sixth in the expected points table for the season.

There is a significant disconnect between performance levels and results, something that usually corrects itself over time. I'm still a firm believer that Oliver Glasner will get this talented group of players motoring up the Premier League table.

And I'm struggling to see why Chelsea should command quite so much respect from the markets.

Of the ever-present Premier League teams in 2026, only one has lost more games than Chelsea (14) and only one has conceded more goals (51).

Where has Xabi Alonso's defensive magic gone?

His invincible Bayer Leverkusen side conceded just 24 league goals across their entire title-winning campaign in 2023/24. Chelsea have shipped 20 in 11 games this season alone. There is a softness to this Chelsea team when opponents turn up the intensity and attack them directly.

Just two clean sheets in their last 27 Premier League games tells a sorry tale.

Forest have the attacking weaponry to expose those defensive deficiencies.

The 29/20 with Sky Bet for a home win makes lots of sense.

When the numbers and the theory marry up in the player fouls markets, I'm usually willing to get stuck in. And there is a lovely little match-up brewing down Leeds' right flank that Sky Bet may have underestimated.

Jayden Bogle is an all-action footballer. He's busy, aggressive and covers plenty of ground, which brings him into contact with opposition players at both ends of the pitch. That is exactly the profile of player I like to get onside in the fouls markets.

Across his last 30 games for Leeds, Bogle is averaging 1.75 fouls per 90 minutes. A solid enough starting point when assessing the 10/11 with Sky Bet for him to commit two or more fouls - but it's the opposition that really gets me excited.

Coventry's Yann Gboho is a foul-drawing maestro.

Across his last 50 appearances for Coventry and Toulouse, the tricky winger has been fouled at a rate of 2.2 per 90 minutes, winning eight fouls across his last three appearances for Coventry.

There is plenty of juice in that 10/11 considering this bet has won in four of Bogle's last five games.

There are certain footballers you want on your side when playing the cards markets. Lisandro Martinez is very much one of them.

The Argentine looks a walking accident at times for Manchester United, such is his desire to engage physically with opposition players. But throw him into a left-back role and his chances of falling foul of the referee increase significantly.

His natural instinct is to get tight and aggressive rather than stand off his opponent - as we saw with the foul he gave away in Sporting Lisbon that led to a penalty. That's a dangerous game to play against someone with the explosive qualities of Dango Ouattara.

The Brentford winger is developing quite the reputation as a card magnet for opposition defenders.

Since the start of the 25/25 season, Ouattara has drawn a card from an opponent every 199 minutes - that's 14 cards in total. Only Crysensio Summerville (118 mins per card) has a better strike-rate.

Those are impressive numbers and his directness with the ball should make for uncomfortable viewing for Martinez. Ouattara was responsible for getting Vitaliy Mykolenko booked in Monday's win over Everton, too.

The 7/2 with Sky Bet for Martinez to have his name taken looks a price worth attacking.

There is a rather large gap between perception and reality when it comes to Ipswich.

Eleven points from 11 games looks a perfectly acceptable return for a newly promoted team. But scratch beneath the surface and things look considerably more worrying.

Ipswich's expected goals supremacy figure of -0.81 per 90 minutes is the second worst in the Premier League. When assessing their performance when matches are level, that figure drops to -0.98 - the worst in the division.

Their reliance on Julio Enciso to provide attacking inspiration is another concern. Shut him down and Ipswich can become painfully predictable.

Enter Unai Emery, who is unbeaten in 10 games away from home against newly promoted opposition with Villa.

There are very few managers I'd rather have onside when backing a team to expose the obvious tactical weaknesses of an opponent. The 10/11 with Sky Bet for the away win is worth taking.

A Merseyside derby before most people have tucked into their Sunday roast? I'm not sure we're going to be treated to a feast of attacking football.

These fixtures rarely deliver in terms of goalmouth entertainment anyway, with the last 14 Merseyside derbies averaging just 2.2 goals per game. And the unusual kick-off time could further contribute to a lack of intensity, both on the pitch and in the stands.

I've dug into the numbers surrounding major English derby fixtures played at this time on a Sunday. Across the seven instances involving the north London derby, the Tyne-Wear derby and Manchester United vs Liverpool kicking off before 12.30pm, under 3.5 goals has landed every time.

It's a small sample but one that marries up nicely with the theory.

To get some juice into the price, I'm adding Alexander Isak to register a shot on target through the Bet Builder, which gets us to Evens with Sky Bet.

Isak is starting to look like the devastating centre-forward we know he can be. He's registered a shot on target in 11 of his last 12 games, including five across his last two.

One of my favourite player markets to attack with Sky Bet is foul involvements when the numbers add up. For those unfamiliar with the market, it's simply a player's fouls committed and fouls won numbers added together. It opens up plenty of opportunities when you can identify a particularly physical individual battle.

And there's one brewing between Luka Vuskovic and Will Osula.

Osula is a proper handful. He's a powerful, willing runner who relishes the physical side of being a centre-forward. Across his last 25 starts, he's averaged 2.70 foul involvements per game.

Throw into the equation a centre-back in Vuskovic who averages 2.72 foul involvements per game for Brighton since joining from Tottenham and we've got all the ingredients for a busy afternoon for the referee.

Anyone who watched Vuskovic's battle with Oliver McBurnie last weekend will know exactly where I'm coming from. It was brutal at times. Vuskovic racked up seven foul involvements as neither player was willing to give an inch.

I'd expect plenty of grappling, shirt-pulling and wrestling when these two come together. Vuskovic's foul involvements is a market worth monitoring with Sky Bet.

The new manager bounce is a rather fluffy concept. But there is some substance to it when digging into the numbers, especially when the new man in the dugout has home advantage.

Backing the home team in each of the last 30 Premier League matches where a newly appointed manager has taken charge of his first game in the competition for that club would have returned a profit of 9.04 points to level stakes, with 14 wins.

But what really got my betting juices flowing was that 10 of those 14 home wins came with a clean sheet.

Why? Well, my hypothesis is that the quickest way for a new manager to put his stamp on a team is to address their defensive structure. Thomas Frank has openly admitted that defensive organisation is high on his list of priorities at Crystal Palace.

And he could hardly have handpicked a more accommodating opponent in that regard.

I've got plenty of respect for Hull and their ability to squeeze results out of games but their attacking process remains the worst in the Premier League. They rank bottom for expected goals, big chances created and touches in the opposition box.

That makes the 5/2 with Sky Bet for Palace to win to nil a very attractive betting proposition. Frank can get the Selhurst Park faithful onside by keeping things simple.

My colleague Adam Bate wrote a fantastic piece about Fulham's man-to-man marking tactics up against Erling Haaland, offering up some huge pointers for us punters who like to dabble in the player fouls and cards markets.

Alvaro Arbeloa wants his defenders to engage, get tight and make life as uncomfortable as possible for opposition forwards, even if that means following them into areas of the pitch where centre-backs wouldn't usually venture.

Calvin Bassey is having a fantastic season playing this way. He's got the physical attributes to thrive in such a system but there is an occupational hazard attached to defending with that level of aggression. He's already picked up four yellow cards this season.

And the identity of his likely opponent here makes the 3/1 with Sky Bet for Bassey to be carded a very appealing price.

Evanilson is a master at using his body to manufacture fouls, inviting contact from defenders before rolling them. Since the start of last season, the Bournemouth striker has drawn a card from an opposition player every 267 minutes.

The Tottenham defensive revolution under Roberto De Zerbi remains one of the more fascinating developments of this Premier League season. There is a perception associated with De Zerbi's football that it will always produce chaotic matches with chances flowing at both ends.

The numbers have been telling a rather different story.

Across his time in charge of Spurs, their expected goals against figure is operating at 1.03 - a figure that ranks them second only to Arsenal over that period. That's a very impressive foundation, particularly for a team whose reputation remains associated with defensive shortcomings.

The absence of European football should increasingly become a significant advantage for Tottenham as the schedule intensifies, too.

Sunderland's attacking troubles make this a particularly attractive opportunity to exploit Spurs' defensive improvement. A Spurs win to nil has a chance at 5/2 with Sky Bet.

Stuart Pearce was in the Manchester City dugout the last time they endured a Premier League run as bad as the one they'll be on if Arsenal beat them here - one point from five games.

City have won inside 90 minutes in just one of their last seven games across all competitions and look horribly vulnerable without the ball.

Stability is proving elusive for Enzo Maresca. He's used eight different back-four combinations across City's last 10 games in all competitions, tinkering with his defensive personnel from one game to the next. Not a single clean sheet has been forthcoming and they've shipped 20 goals in that period.

Arsenal are worthy favourites but the way to inject some juice into their price is through Noni Madueke.

He's grasped the opportunity presented to him by Bukayo Saka's absence. What he did to Lewis Hall at St James' Park was particularly impressive considering the Newcastle full-back had kept Lamine Yamal relatively quiet for England just a few days earlier.

There is an explosiveness to Madueke's game that makes him capable of creating chances without Arsenal having to dominate territory or possession - something that should be particularly valuable here.

He's registered a goal or assist in three of his last four games. Combining that outcome with an Arsenal win at 15/8 with Sky Bet appeals greatly.

#830. Tosin Adarabioyo: ‘No one can chat s*** about Cole Palmer’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Interview: Adarabioyo, speaking at the launch of his trading card shop, issued a passionate defence of his former Chelsea team-mate Palmer amid criticism of his attitude

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Tosin Adarabioyo has leapt to the defence of former Chelsea team-mate Cole Palmer amid criticism of the Englishman’s attitude.

Palmer came under fire for a viral interaction with Joao Pedro after Chelsea’s bruising 4-1 thrashing by Leeds last weekend, brushing off the Brazilian after opting not to acknowledge the home fans who booed the team at full-time.

The 24-year-old is going through a difficult patch at the moment, having been left out of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad again for the November internationals after the German manager claimed “he misses too opportunities to impress”.

This led to questions over Palmer’s commitment to the England cause, something club team-mate Morgan Rogers emphatically refuted as “nonsense” and “a lie”.

And Tosin, who moved to from Chelsea to rivals Tottenham in the summer, has now become the latest to publicly back Palmer, with whom he shared two seasons at Stamford Bridge.

“No one can chat s*** about Cole,” Tosin said.

“For me, he's one of the best players I've ever seen. You can say what you want. Honestly, you guys can say what you want. He's a top level player. He will continue to get better.”

Asked whether he was surprised about Palmer’s omission from the England squad, he replied: “Yeah, for sure. Of course, I'm surprised. For me, he's the best No 10 in the Premier League.”

Tosin also echoed Rogers’ sentiment in regards to doubts over Palmer’s hunger to play for the Three Lions, with the Chelsea forward struggling to get back in favour with Tuchel after missing out on the World Cup, before his return to the international fold in September was swiftly curtailed by injury.

“False, false, false,” Tosin added. “I know Cole's dreams, his aspirations. So, yeah, it's completely false.”

While Tosin will passionately defend Palmer against his critics, this doesn’t spare the Chelsea man of a friendly jibe, especially in the wake of Tottenham’s first win at Stamford Bridge in eight years last month.

Palmer was sent off in the 2-0 defeat to their fierce rivals and Tosin, who missed the match through injury, was sure to savour the triumph at his mate’s expense.

Asked if the pair shared some post-match banter, Tosin laughed: “Cole's my guy, man - yeah, of course. But I'll keep that secret.”

Palmer was among a number of Tosin’s team-mates, past and present, supporting him at the launch of his trading card shop, Card Cop, in London. The retail space in Borough Yards will open to the public on Thursday 26 November.

The Spurs defender, who is an avid collector, is joined by the likes of former Blues team-mates Reece James and Levi Colwill, as well as West Ham defender Kyle Walker-Peters, in investing in the business.

Along with the investors, Chelsea’s contingent at the launch party included Rogers, Emmanuel Emegha and Jamie Gittens, while the likes of Dominic Solanke, Micky van de Ven, Archie Gray and Ben Davies came down to support their relatively new Spurs colleague.

“It’s a testament to what we're like as a team,” Tosin said. “We're all very close and very supportive of each other. The boys didn't have to turn up today, but they did. It's amazing. I'm very thankful to them.”

After a dire start to the season, feeling the hangover of their near-miss with relegation last term, Spurs have finally found their groove under Roberto De Zerbi and are now just one point off Chelsea after four wins in five.

Tosin puts the uptick in form down to the team’s Marbella training camp during the first international break of the season, which was crucial in forming a bond within the team.

“It's our trip to Marbella,” he said. “We had a great time. We bonded together. We learned a lot about each other, and we're all striving to put this club where we think it belongs.”

Manchester United's No.1 was dependable last season - but hasn't seemed himself this term

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There were other factors that led to Manchester United’s 4-0 defeat to Liverpool besides Senne Lammens’ performance, like Leny Yoro’s red card after only eight minutes. Down to 10 men for the majority of the match, Mauricio Pochettino’s debut as manager became about damage limitation from that point on.

And yet in the post-match analysis, Manchester United’s first-choice goalkeeper still found himself scrutinised. “If he’s in the right position, he saves it comfortably,” argued Danny Murphy on Match of the Day, highlighting Lammens’ positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opener.

It wasn’t the first time a Lammens mistake has been highlighted this season. While the Belgian was widely hailed for his performances in his debut Premier League campaign after joining from Royal Antwerp, the malaise around him at Old Trafford has dragged him down. He, like many of his United teammates, is under-performing.

Before the November international break, Lammens was blamed for two goals in the chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, too easily beaten at his near post by Alysson for Villa’s first and spilling a shot for Nicolas Jackson to make it 2-0 after only four minutes. He was shaky throughout.

There was also Lammens’ ill-judged decision to come rushing off his line against Bournemouth, giving Evanilson the chance to finish into an empty net in a 3-0 win for the Cherries at Old Trafford. The messy own goal conceded by Manchester United in the 1-1 draw away to Fulham was another that involved Lammens.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence. His struggles can be traced back to the World Cup where he made a blunder that led to Belgium’s exit from the tournament, spilling a shot for Mikel Merino to score a late winner for Spain. Lammens hasn’t been the same since that moment.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There are, however, some mitigating factors to explain the goalkeeper’s form. For starters, Lammens is having to make more saves this season. Last season, the 24-year-old averaged 2.4 saves per 90 minutes in the Premier League, whereas this season that number has increased to 3.6 saves per 90 minutes.

Only Crystal Palace have conceded more Expected Goals (xG) in the Premier League this season than Manchester United. Lammens is being afforded very little protection by the players in front of him, as demonstrated by United’s shambolic defensive performance at Anfield on Sunday.

For comparison, Manchester United conceded the fourth-lowest xG over the course of the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Their sudden defensive drop-off is somewhat unexplainable, but it goes a long way to reasoning why Lammens is struggling so much. He’s simply having to do more. He’s being overwhelmed.

Lammens hasn’t actually regressed much in terms of his save percentage. This season, the Belgian is ranked 16th in the Premier League for this metric, whereas last season he was 14th. Lammens has never been anywhere near the most effective shot-stoppers in this regard.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence

It’s possible Lammens over-performed last season. Without the Belgian settling so quickly after arriving as an emergency upgrade on Andre Onana and Altay Bayindir, it’s difficult to envisage Manchester United finishing third. His saves did a lot to mask some of United’s structural deficiencies.

No goalkeeper in the Premier League last season prevented more goals than Lammens (6.4). That ranked him ahead of the likes of Gianluigi Donnarumma, Emi Martinez, Jordan Pickford, Alisson Becker and David Raya. It was perhaps unrealistic to expect someone still so young in goalkeeper years to maintain such a high level.

“This break came at the ideal moment for me,” said Lammens in the last international break during which he played the full 90 minutes in back-to-back games for Belgium against Turkey and Italy, saving a penalty against the latter. “These have been difficult weeks for me at Manchester United.”

Life for Lammens didn’t get any easier in his first match back from international duty, although the Belgian’s seven saves prevented the scoreline from being even more humiliating for Manchester United. There were moments when Lammens showed the sort of form that made him so eye-catching last season.

Pochettino might find a way to steady Manchester United at the back. The Argentine set up the Old Trafford outfit with a back three in possession before Yoro’s red card completely changed the dynamic of the match. With 11 men on the pitch, Pochettino should find it easier to implement a defensive game plan, although that’s something Michael Carrick never managed.

This could help Lammens rediscover his best form. If not, Manchester United will need their goalkeeper to eliminate the errors from his performances on his own accord, otherwise a relegation scrap at the bottom of the Premier League table could be unavoidable. Lammens can’t count on getting any more help any time soon.

#827. Dominic Calvert-Lewin signs new Leeds deal

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The England international has extended his stay with the club until 2029

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal, taking his stay with the club until 2029.

The England international joined Leeds on a three-year deal after leaving Everton as a free agent in 2025, and has now extended for another two and a half years.

He scored 15 goals in all competitions last season and so far has six in this campaign, having rebooted his career following a difficult spell marred by injuries at Everton, and earned a recall to the England squad.

Leeds said: “Leeds United are delighted to announce Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new contract with the club.

“The England international has put pen to paper on a two-and-a-half-year deal at Elland Road, keeping him in West Yorkshire until the summer of 2029.

“Everyone at Leeds United is thrilled Dominic has signed a new deal and we look forward to seeing him continue to impress in the famous white shirt.”

Calvert-Lewin has started all 11 top-flight fixtures of this season and scored in the statement 4-1 victory over Chelsea on Saturday. Leeds currently sit seventh in the Premier League, four points off the Champions League places.

He won the Premier League’s Player of the Month Award in December after scoring in six consecutive matches - becoming the first Leeds player to win the award in 24 years.

His performances were recognised by Thomas Tuchel, who called him up to international duty for a 1-1 friendly draw with Uruguay in March, and he retained his place the squad for Nations League matches against Spain and Czechia.

His latest England appearance was against Spain earlier this month when he stepped off the bench to win his 15th cap in the Three Lions’ 3-2 win.
