#826. Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

Never before have young people around the world been so well-educated while facing so many economic challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

This article was originally published in German.

#824. 'Losing respect for him' - Pundits react to stunning Rodgers claims

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers claims that head coach Mike McCarthy was 'snoring' in a quarterback meeting in an explosive interview; Steelers president Art Rooney II comes out in "100 per cent" support of McCarthy after team releases Rodgers in light of comments

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Has Aaron Rodgers played his final game in the NFL? Was he wrong to publicly criticise Mike McCarthy? The four-time MVP quarterback is 'losing respect' following his explosive claims about the Pittsburgh Steelers head coach, according to Sky Sports NFL's Jason Bell.

Rodgers sent shockwaves through the NFL on Thanksgiving Eve as he used an interview on The Pat McAfee Show to claim McCarthy had been "falling asleep in meetings" while suggesting his entire team believed a change was required on the sideline.

It came after Rodgers was benched for Friday's matchup with the Denver Broncos following two straight defeats, with Mason Rudolph due to start under center.

The Steelers later released Rodgers 11 weeks into what is set to be the final season of the 42-year-old's career.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"First of all, I don't want to be on Aaron Rodgers' bad side. Let's start there. We all make mistakes, right? We all do things that aren't necessarily right in the moment," said Sky Sports NFL's Bell.

"But when I look at him as a player, he wasn't playing well. He wasn't helping his team.

"And you could could see him and his head coach arguing on the sideline with with each other. They weren't getting along.

Sky Sports NFL pundits tuck into their Thanksgiving turkey!

"Whatever happens behind closed doors, that goes down, but the response to it is where I'm losing a little respect.

"In that locker room is a sanctuary. Some things we just don't let out. We don't have those conversations in public - it's a respect thing.

"If Rodgers was playing MVP football like he did before, he could say all these things and get away with it, but you have to know where you are in your career."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rodgers suggested in his appearance on The Pat McAfee Show that the prospect of being benched had never been mentioned during recent conversations with McCarthy.

He accused McCarthy of snoring during meetings and rebuffing Rodgers' suggestions that he needed to make more of an effort of connecting with the Steelers' defensive players.

Rodgers added that the "final straw" came during half-time of a game when McCarthy closed a team talk by shouting 'one, two, three, Packers!'.

Rodgers and McCarthy spent 13 seasons together with the Packers from 2006-2018, reaching the playoffs nine times and winning one Super Bowl. They were reunited this past offseason when the Steelers hired McCarthy following the departure of Mike Tomlin.

"I'm not sure what's next for Aaron Rodgers. I think he will figure out that for himself over the next handful of months, or whatever his particular process is," said Super Bowl champion and Sky Sports NFL expert Ndamukong Suh.

"But I want to go back to what Jason [Bell] said in the way that you handle your business, especially from the perspective of a star. There's a way you go about handling things.

"Those things should be handled behind closed doors before trying to get ahead of the story - on either side. Have a conversation, have an understanding, and then go from there and address it.

"Going out to the media and doing all of these different things, The Pat McAfee Show, it's great for them and great for ESPN, but it's not the proper way I would want to handle that particular scenario."

Responding to Rodgers' comments, McCarthy admitted to his "embarrassing" moment when mentioning the Packers during half-time of their defeat to the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 11.

Steelers president Art Rooney II defended McCarthy on Thursday in an interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, insisting he supports him "100 per cent".

"I just want to say that I have 100 per cent confidence in Mike McCarthy and I expect he'll be our coach this season, next season and beyond," Mr Rooney II told the Post-Gazette.

"The big thing, what happened this week, is insubordination can't be tolerated in any organization. When you start getting ultimatums, you can't live with that. There's maybe a time and place after the season if he wanted to kind of unload.

"He talks about wanting to be a good teammate, but you don't do that to your teammates a couple days before the game, that's for sure."

Rooney II underlined his belief that events in the locker room should be kept within the locker room, and downplayed Rodgers' comments regarding concerns for McCarthy's health.

The Steelers are 6-4 as they prepare to face the Denver Broncos (8-2) on Black Friday.

Kelly Somers shares her favourite post-match moments as the BBC's in-camp England reporter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kelly Somers has recalled a deeply personal moment with Sir Gareth Southgate after England’s victory over Germany at Euro 2020 – and a thoughtful gesture the former Three Lions manager made when she was pregnant.

Sir Gareth's England beat Germany 2-0 at Wembley in June 2021, 25 years after his decisive penalty miss against the same opponents in the Euro 96 semi-finals, and the result prompted an emotional reflection on the team-mates he felt he had let down all those years ago.

As the BBC’s England reporter, Somers was there to capture that reaction, and says it remains one of the standout conversations of her time following the national side.

Asked for her favourite interviews over her years covering England, Somers told FourFourTwo: “[Southgate] said he’d looked up to the big screen midway through the game and seen David Seaman sitting there.

“He said 'I know I can never undo any of the heartache I caused them, but hopefully this has gone a long way'. Hearing him say that was really special.”

Somers was also touched by an off-camera gesture delivered by Southgate during her pregnancy in 2023.

She said: “When I was pregnant in 2023, Gareth gave me a little England kit for my daughter in a gift bag.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“In true Gareth Southgate fashion, he said 'I didn’t actually know about your pregnancy, my team arranged this, but this is on behalf of the FA'.

"He didn’t want to take the credit for it, which I thought was lovely.”

Somers also picked out interviewing Ollie Watkins dramatic winner against the Netherlands in the Euro 2024 semi-final as a highlight.

She said: "It felt like I was talking to a boy from the park, I was speaking to someone at pretty much the pinnacle of their life.

“There was another where I had to wait for Jude Bellingham after a drugs test, and he came out in just his top and pants. I thought ‘This is all very weird!’ But he’s always very good in interviews."

Somers added: "To be the in-camp reporter is incredible, because pretty much every day you get 15 minutes with a different player, so I’ve got to know them. I love interviewing and the challenge of bringing out the human side of players.

"At the Euros in 2021, I did one with Jack Grealish where he spoke about his sister – he’s incredibly close to his family. When the interview ended, he said “I was getting emotional, I didn’t expect that.”

When Hotels.com asked FourFourTwo if we'd like to see a Real Madrid game, we happily accepted - especially when we realised how much we'd pack into the trip

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Be nice to people on your way up, because you'll meet them on your way down – whether you're Wayne Rooney at Everton, Theo Walcott at Southampton or just expecting to queue with the same crowd on a return flight from Madrid.

It's 8am on a Saturday though, and while plenty of the punters have dropped off luggage, FourFourTwo are doing no such thing, travelling light for a hit-and-run mission to Spain: yep, we're coming back here tomorrow.

Welcome to the era of 'Trip Snacking': the only sights we're taking in are Jose Mourinho's thousand-yard stare, Jude Bellingham's outstretched arms and the wonder of learning that Iago Aspas, pushing 40, is still getting wheeled out on the biggest stages of all. We're here for a prime cut of La Liga, and this time, you can keep your museums, palaces and fancy sky bars.

FourFourTwo have always loved a quick turnaround – the relentless nature of European away days practically dictates it – but the concept has officially gone mainstream. According to Hotels.com’s Unpack ’27 travel trends report, Trip Snacking is the defining travel trend of 2027. It's the rise of the one-night stay – the loan spell of the tourism world – precision-engineered to fit seamlessly around packed schedules and tighter budgets, with fans increasingly turning match-day into getaway-day. Count us in.

The numbers speak for themselves. Searches for one-night stays are up nearly 10 per cent year-on-year globally, and up 15 per cent among British travellers. Some 73 per cent of travellers booked a one-night stay in the past 12 months, and 79 per cent say they are planning to book one in the coming year, climbing to 83 per cent among Millennials and Gen Z.

While 42 per cent cite celebrating life milestones and 23 per cent simply need a quick reset between traditional holidays, a massive 49 per cent of Brits are doing it to attend concerts, shows and sporting events.

That's why we're here. Madrid is one of the biggest beneficiaries of the trend: weekend lodging searches to the Spanish capital during the football season are up 20 per cent year-on-year, while full-season searches have risen 25 per cent. It's a pattern repeating across Europe's major footballing hubs – demand has surged in Liverpool (up 100 per cent), Manchester (up 95 per cent), London (up 40 per cent) and Munich (up 10 per cent). Unsurprisingly, marquee European nights drive the biggest spikes, with Madrid searches jumping 70 per cent around a clash with Bayern Munich, and Manchester rising 25 per cent when Los Blancos came to town.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

As an Official Partner of Real Madrid, Hotels.com arranged our stay at the five-star Barcelo Imagine – one of their top-rated picks for a Madrid football break, starting at £125 per night – purely for Real hosting Celta Vigo at the Bernabeu. On a 24-hour getaway, staying close to the action is half the battle.

A quick drop of the bags and we're out into the crisp Madrid afternoon. It's warm for November, ideal for a stroll up towards the Bernabeu, semi-newly renovated – looking a little like a giant airfryer – and packed with fans and tourists alike. Thanks to our hosts, FourFourTwo took in the action from the Hotels.com VIP box, situated just behind the goal. The PA system is booming – a little like we imagine Mourinho will be when Real return to the dressing room for the half-time break trailing by a goal. But we came here to have superstars, and the Special One appears obliging to treat us to a fair few from his bench.

A beautiful five-star hotel just a five-minute Uber from the Bernabeu, the Barcelo Imagine is a superb choice to stay at for Trip snacking. The seasonal outdoor pool is a great spot to take a dip, and guests can grab a bite to eat at Eat & Roll, which serves local and international cuisine and is open for breakfast. Other highlights at this luxurious hotel include 2 bars/lounges, a poolside bar and a fitness centre

Vinicius Jr has struggled early on this season but is now back to his sparkling best, grabbing the game by the scruff of the neck and toying with his full-back like a cat with string. Pretty soon after his introduction, the stadium is dancing to a samba rhythm, led by the Brazilian orchestrating with ease – and after Bellingham's punchy equaliser, Los Blancos really step up a gear. It's a lesser-known name, Carlos Espi, who grabs the winner from close range, letting out a primal roar in front of the Grada Fans, reflecting 80,000 relieved Madridistas, all exhaling at once.

In the end, Celta simply couldn't keep up, as we discuss after the game. This is where the true joy of the Madrid Trip Snack begins: a late dinner means midnight tapas, swapping stories, and dissecting the match over plates of jamon iberico and patatas bravas. Some 32 per cent of travellers say they have taken a one-night trip specifically for a sporting event – rising to 33 per cent among women – and turning a 90-minute match into a 24-hour cultural immersion feels like the ultimate life hack.

As Melanie Fish, Hotels.com spokesperson and travel expert, puts it: "Football fans aren't waiting for a week-long holiday anymore. They're turning matches into memorable 24-hour getaways, whether that's a weekend in Madrid or a European away game." For Trip Snackers, finding a good deal is key, and perks like free cancellation and earning £100 in Hotels.comCash after 10 nights make squeezing in a spontaneous trip much easier to justify.

Sunday morning allows for no such gentle reset – we're going back to the Bernabeu for a tour of the stadium, believe it or not – before heading off to the airport, roughly 24 hours after we arrived. We feel a little like an away team, jetting into the city just for the game, enjoying a warm down and getting back for Match of the Day 2 – but we crammed in enough football, croquettes and merch from the Real club shop that it feels like we were away longer than just a day.

An impressive 71 per cent of travellers agree that a Trip Snack holds them over until their next longer trip, and it is easy to see why. We do not always have the time, the annual leave, or the funds for a sprawling European tour. We cannot all travel the continent watching our team – especially when it's Real Madrid, who have been to Rome and Athens already this autumn, with London on tfhotelshe horizon.

Sometimes, you just need a quick fix. Sometimes it takes heading to the nation of tapas to realise you just need a bite over a buffet.

#821. Brighton bounce back with Conference League win as Hearts suffer last-gasp defeat

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Osman scored twice and set up another for Charalampos Kostoulas in a 4-0 win

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ibrahim Osman scored his first Brighton goals as his side returned to winning ways by cruising to a 4-0 success over 10-man Universitatea Craiova in the Conference League.

Talk of the high-flying Seagulls potentially being shock Premier League title contenders this season was dampened slightly by Sunday’s surprise 2-0 defeat at Hull.

But Brighton were back to their best against Romanian champions Craiova at the Amex Stadium, with winger Osman putting the Seagulls ahead in the third minute.

Jack Hinshelwood stepped over the ball following Ferdi Kadioglu’s low cross from the right before being played in by Charalampos Kostoulas and squaring to leave Osman with a simple tap-in.

Matt O’Riley had the ball in the net in the 27th minute but the effort was ruled out for offside against Chema Andres, but Maxim De Cuyper scored Brighton’s second six minutes later.

Things went from bad to worse for Craiova, who currently sit top of their domestic league, as defender Vladimir Screciu was sent off in the 39th minute for stamping on O’Riley’s ankle.

Osman set up Kostoulas for the third goal before quickly claiming his second with a fine individual effort as Brighton made it 10 points from four games in the competition.

The 21-year-old should have had another assist but his inviting low cross was blazed over the open goal by substitute Femi Azeez, who later curled narrowly wide.

Azeez’s glaring miss mattered little as Brighton comfortably extended their unbeaten home record to eight games ahead of attempting to put the league campaign back on track when Newcastle visit on Sunday.

Elsewhere on Thursday night Hearts’ Conference League hopes suffered a hammer blow as Folarin Balogun’s stoppage-time goal consigned them to a 3-2 defeat at home to Monaco.

Theylooked on course to pick up their second league-phase point after stunning first-half strikes from Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota either side of goals from visiting pair Folarin Balogun and Edian Diop.

But in the last of four added minutes, USA forward Balogun got himself free in the box to slot home and maintain Monaco’s perfect record in the competition.

Hearts will now require high-scoring victories over Borac and Pafos in their last two games to have a chance of scrambling into the top 24 and qualifying for the knockout phase.

One Arsenal star is in talks to leave the club, despite getting the nod last night to start against Borussia Dortmund.

The Gunners were held to a 1-1 draw by the Bundesliga leaders last night, despite creating a plethora of chances, finding themselves needing two wins from their next three Champions League fixtures to finish in the top eight of the league phase.

But despite Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta making six changes last night, one star is still “unhappy” and seeking an exit from N5.

Criticised at times during his tenure at the Emirates Stadium for a lack of rotation, Arteta seems to have changed approach this term and given more game time to his squad players.

Riccardo Calafiori and Kai Havertz were both unused substitutes last night against Dortmund, Ben White and Jurrien Timber have shared the right-back position, and Myles Lewis-Skelly has had ample opportunities despite the signing of Bruno Guimaraes.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, however, is “unhappy” with his role within the squad, with Sport Witness relaying a report from Spanish outlet El Desmarque that Valencia have approached the goalkeeper.

The most expensive goalkeeper of all time joined the Gunners in 2025 on a cut-price deal from Chelsea, following loans at Real Madrid and Bournemouth – and despite serving as the first choice at Dean Court, he has largely been a cup keeper for the Gunners.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Despite getting his chance last night, and as a substitute against Newcastle United at the weekend when David Raya went off injured, Arrizabalaga hasn't troubled his fellow Spaniard for the No.1 jersey, with the champions signing French custodian Ilian Meslier over the summer, too.

This new report states that the Basque is “unhappy with his secondary role at Arsenal”, and “eager to return” to La Liga, following rumours that he would depart over the summer after just a season in North London.

A move is described as “complicated”, however, with Arsenal unwilling to let the star go.

Arsenal have signed a goalkeeper every year since Arteta took the reins, with the likes of Mat Ryan, Aaron Ramsdale, Matt Turner and Neto all joining the club and leaving since 2019.

The Premier League champions have several good prospects between the sticks, too, with Tommy Setford on loan at Stevenage, academy prospect Jack Porter well thought of and Dane Lucas Nygaard having joined at the age of 18 in June 2024.

Arrizabalaga is worth €5 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal host Manchester City this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

Tottenham Hotspur are resurgent in the Premier League – but that hasn't stopped one player's agent from linking his client with a move out of N17.

FourFourTwo understands that Spurs don't expect to do very much business in the winter window, with the likes of Jan Paul van Hecke, Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Savio and Omar Marmoush signed over the summer in a £400 million spree that saw Tottenham smash their transfer record twice.

But while the summer saw significant departures, there could well be more where that came from this January, with one star publicly angling to leave.

The Lilywhites have won four of their last five fixtures in the league and turned their form around, as they look to bounce back from back-to-back 17th-placed finishes.

With plenty of interest in Al-Ahli striker Ivan Toney from the likes of Manchester United and Newcastle, however, Spurs could see an opportunity to move on a wantaway fringe player from their squad.

Sport Witness have relayed an interview from Al-Maidan with Richarlison’s agent, Fidel Carvalho Soares, in which the Brazilian has been mentioned as a target for the Saudi Pro League.

Richarlison came close to an exit over the summer from the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium but after the transfer fell through, he hasn't played under manager Roberto De Zerbi this term, with his future at the club to be decided in January.

“What is being said about negotiations between Al-Ahli and the player are just rumours,” Soares said, “However, Richarlison would welcome the opportunity to play in the Saudi league soon.

The agent added that Trabzonspor made an official offer over the summer but after the North Londoners rejected the bid, the Turkish side haven't been in contact again to rekindle the embers of a move.

The 29-year-old joined Spurs in 2022 in a deal that The Guardian reported as being worth £60 million at the time, after a successful 2021/22 season in which his 10 goals helped keep Everton in the Premier League.

Despite hitting double figures in the league twice in the capital, however, the forward has struggled for consistency and was omitted from Carlo Ancelotti's Brazil squad for the 2026 World Cup after leading the line for the Selecao at the last edition of the competition in Qatar four years earlier.

Richarlison is worth €15 million, according to Transfermarkt. Spurs travel to Sunderland this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

#817. A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains. Credit: 3DMedisphere/SPL

In the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

Although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

Scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

“We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” says Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in New York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”

This year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very important milestone,” says Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

Success is by no means guaranteed, says Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” says Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

The latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” says Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City.

Starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” says Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

One overarching problem, says Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

That attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” says Burton.

Researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, says Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

To mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

Source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Sanders says that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, says virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

In small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” says Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

#816. Europa League match suspended after police clashes over Palestine banner

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute and restarted 30 minutes later

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Europa League game between Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for around 30 minutes on Thursday when police clashed with fans of the Turkish club after they displayed a banner in support of Palestine.

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute but restarted after the interruption.

Turkey’s Haberturk broadcaster said Georgian police used pepper spray against the Besiktas fans, who also unfurled a Palestinian flag, prompting referee referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

In a statement, Besiktas accused the Georgian security forces of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

Georgian police entered the stands and ⁠used pepper spray on Besiktas fans, Turkish outlet NTV reported.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the club said. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”

The report added that Turkish fans chanted “Down with Israel” and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters before play restarted to calm the situation.

The Turkish Football Federation condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters on X, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination. It said it would press for an investigation.

The TFF’s statement read: “We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, conduct and interference directed at Beşiktaş supporters, both inside and outside the stadium, before and during our club’s UEFA Europa League match against Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia.

“No practice that disregards the universal values of sport, human dignity, mutual respect and the principles of fair play, or that involves discrimination, exclusion or security failures, can be tolerated.

“Nor can there be any question of remaining silent in the face of such conduct, which endangers our supporters’ safety and targets their fundamental rights and freedoms.

“As the Turkish Football Federation, we declare unequivocally that we will follow this matter to its conclusion to ensure that the events are fully investigated, those responsible are identified and the necessary sanctions are imposed without delay.

“There must be no tolerance for covering up these events, allowing those responsible to evade accountability or permitting similar violations to recur.

“We emphasize that we stand firmly with our club, Beşiktaş, and our supporters, who faced a series of problems, particularly serious security failures, and extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our supporters subjected to interference and mistreatment.

“Let no one forget that we will not remain silent in the face of disrespect, discrimination and security violations directed at representatives and supporters of Turkish football.

“We will act decisively on national and international platforms to ensure that all necessary steps are taken, particularly with UEFA, and that those responsible are held accountable.”

Fenerbache also posted in support of their Turkish rivals.

The ⁠officiating team and the Besiktas players ‌left ​the pitch before ‌the game restarted.

Earlier, the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva and Israel FA had not commented on the incident at the time of publishing.

Manchester City started brightly under Enzo Maresca, but after terrible form of late, the club are considering the Italian's future

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester City are considering the future of manager Enzo Maresca, just 19 games into the Italian's stint.

After Pep Guardiola led the Citizens to 20 trophies in a decade-long tenure, Manchester City turned to Maresca to take charge of the club, with the former Leicester City and Chelsea boss having worked at the Etihad as both the under-23s manager and as one of Guardiola's assistants in the 2022/23 Treble-winning campaign.

But with uncertainty shrouding the club – following an independent commission finding City guilty of over 100 breaches of serious financial rules across a nine-year period – things may be about to become even more unstable, should the six-time Premier League champions pull the trigger on their manager already.

Maresca started fantastically after taking over from his former mentor, winning his first seven Premier League games – including a defiant 3-0 thumping of Liverpool at Anfield following the news that City had been found guilty and were facing Premier League sanctions.

But the Eastlands outfit went on to lose the following three games in the league, drew against Fulham at the weekend, and had to rely on a late Rayan Cherki equaliser against Napoli last night in order to scrape a point in the Champions League.

Fichajes in Spain are reporting that Maresca “will be fighting for his job” if he doesn't beat Arsenal this weekend, with the Gunners having already outclassed his side 3-0 in the Community Shield earlier this season.

A defeat at the Emirates Stadium would widen the gap between the pair to a seemingly unassailable nine points, with Liverpool and surprise package Brighton & Hove Albion shaping up to be the champions' biggest threats in completing back-to-back league championships for the first time in almost a century.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While City started the season emphatically, fans have questioned several tactical decisions – and after netting seven in his first seven fixtures, talismanic centre-forward Erling Haaland has cut a frustrated figure while leading the line.

Record signing Enzo Fernandez has blown hot and cold this season and kept the mercurial Cherki out of the side at times, Marc Guehi has started the season slowly with shaky performances from centre-back, and Phil Foden has been in disappointing form in the league, though he netted a hat-trick against AEK Athens in the Champions League.

Several of Guardiola's generals have been linked with exits, with Haaland's future in doubt, while Barcelona have interest in Josko Gvardiol to fill a problem position at left-back.

Despite the autumnal wobble, however, FourFourTwo understands that there are no plans at present to part with Maresca.

The Italian was handed a three-year deal over the summer to succeed Guardiola, with BBC Sport reporting that City paid around £17 million to Maresca's former club Chelsea as a compensation fee after he left the Blues in January 2026, following run of just one win in seven league games.

City's clash with Arsenal is set for 4.30pm this Sunday as Premier League action resumes.

Liverpool and Bayern Munich might be about to shake hands on an intriguing transfer move in which big names move on either side.

The last two summers have been two of the biggest transfer windows in Liverpool's history, with three £100 million players joining the club in a recruitment revolution, following the end of the Jurgen Klopp era.

And things might be about to get even more extraordinary, with Bayern Munich “increasingly likely” to sell one of their biggest names – and the Reds front and centre for his signature.

Despite critics pointing to a lack of balance in their forward options over the summer, Liverpool are starting to find rhythm in attack under new manager Andoni Iraola, as the likes of Bradley Barcola, Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Rio Ngumoha all performed well in the weekend's 4-1 victory over Manchester United.

With Wirtz and Ngumoha both targets of Bayern Munich, however, the balance may be about to shift again – with the Bavarians now “increasingly likely” to sell Jamal Musiala.

Musiala has struggled this season with what he has described as “neurological dysfunction” this season, with honourary Bayern president Uli Hoeness has faced significant criticism for comments in which he questioned whether Musiala will ever return to his best form for Die Roten, stating, “What he is capable of delivering now is no longer what was stipulated in the contract” he signed at the Allianz Arena.

TEAMtalk reports that Liverpool and Arsenal are now interested in Musiala, with Bayern now potentially open to selling a previously untouchable asset – paving the way for either Wirtz or Ngumoha to leave.

It has recently been suggested in the German media that Wirtz and Musiala aren't naturally compatible in the same team, with journalist Christian Falk likening the pair's jostling for a place as Die Mannschaft's No.10 as similar to the battle between Gunter Netzer and Wolfgang Overath for a place in West Germany's 1974 World Cup side.

Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard, meanwhile, has been linked with a move to Bayern – while the Gunners could field Musiala on the left wing.

#812. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

Aston Villa signed Alejandro Garnacho over the summer on loan - but the Argentine winger clearly isn't trusted by Unai Emery

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Aston Villa star Alejandro Garnacho is looking increasingly bereft in the Midlands following comments from manager Unai Emery.

After three wins in their opening three Champions League fixtures, Aston Villa have now lost their last two, with a 1-0 defeat to Galatasaray following the loss against Barcelona – and with Paris Saint-Germain and Borussia Dortmund on the horizon, the Europa League winners face an increasingly tough ask to finish within the league phase's top eight and avoid a play-off place.

It doesn't look hopeful for Garnacho to be involved in either match, following Emery's post-match comments in Istanbul.

TEAMtalk have described the Basque boss's 19-word statement on Garnacho's absence as “humiliating”, when asked about why the winger was excluded from the squad to face Gala.

Garnacho was once labelled as an exciting talent at Manchester United, but was shipped out to Chelsea at the start of last season in a move that would net the Red Devils pure profit on his sale, and failed to light up Stamford Bridge last season – before joining Villa on loan over the summer.

Despite this, the 22-year-old has played just seven times under Emery, all off the bench, with the Villa boss saying after the game, “Today the players who were here are who I think are the best players to be here with us.”

Garnacho will make his move permanent if he makes a certain number of appearances for the Villans this season, as he looks to replace Morgan Rogers, who left Villa Park for a club-record nine-figure fee over the summer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

But rather like Liverpool's Harvey Elliott last term, the winger hasn't impressed Emery in his limited showings, having clocked up 96 forgettable minutes thus far in claret-and-blue.

Elliott played just four times in the Premier League under Emery after it became clear that the five-time Europa League-winning coach didn't see a place in his team for the England under-21 star.

Emery later described the loan move as “embarrassing for everyone involved”, publicly apologising to the player for a move that he believed stunted his development as a midfielder.

FourFourTwo understands that Villa are already looking to back out of a permanent transfer for Garnacho, who moved to Villa along with Nicolas Jackson from the Blues.

These deals are just two of a plethora between the two clubs in recent years, including Jadon Sancho, Axel Disasi, Ian Maatsen, Emiliano Martinez, Carney Chukwuemeka and Omari Kellyman, with both sides criticised for exploiting the Premier League's Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR).

Transfermarkt values Garnacho at €22m. Villa play Ipswich Town away this weekend, as Premier League action continues.

#810. Calvert-Lewin signs new Leeds deal

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal until the summer of 2029 at Leeds; the striker joined the club in 2025 from Everton; he has scored six goals in all competitions this season; his form earned him a recall to the England squad

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal at Leeds, keeping him at the club until the summer of 2029.

Sky Sports News has been reporting that he was expected to commit his future to the club, which has now been confirmed.

Manchester United had shown interest in the 29-year-old.

Calvert-Lewin joined Leeds on a free transfer in the summer of 2025 after leaving Everton. He scored 15 goals across all competitions last season, and has scored six this season. He scored in a 4-1 win against Chelsea on Saturday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Since he joined Leeds, Calvert-Lewin is the highest-scoring Englishman in the Premier League (19) - three ahead of his next closest countrymen, Morgan Gibbs-White and Ollie Watkins.

His form for Leeds saw him return to the England set-up in March, and he also featured in the September/October and November squads. Calvert-Lewin was not selected for the World Cup.

Ao Tanaka is also close to signing a new contract with Leeds, Sky Sports News understands.

The midfielder is understood to have agreed terms on a deal that will keep him at Elland Road until 2029. The 28-year-old's current contract was due to expire in the summer of 2028.

Tanaka has grown to become a key figure in Daniel Farke's side this season, starting in nine of Leeds' 11 Premier League matches. They have lost just 10 of the 66 games Tanaka has started since then.

Calvert-Lewin follows in the footsteps of Ethan Ampadu, Joe Rodon, Jayden Bogle and Brenden Aaronson, who all signed new deals in the summer. Leeds are also reportedly set to trigger Lukas Nmecha's one-year extension.

Leeds are seventh in the Premier League, four points from the Champions League places. They face Coventry next in the league on Saturday.

Ahead of the weekend's match, Daniel Farke has refused to shed any more light on his own new contract talks. He signed a four-year contract when appointed in 2023 and that is set to expire at the end of the season.

He was reported to have parted company with his agent in October while reaching an agreement with Leeds in principle to extend his contract until 2029.

Farke said: "I'm the manager of Leeds United. I sign players. I don't sign managers. Since I've been here, I fell in love with the people here, and I fell in love with the club.

"And the only thing I care for is our supporters because they had to suffer really for such a long time. I want to bring success to them. I care for the players, I care for the staff and this is the way I work.

"I think this is also the reason I don't like to talk about my contract at all because I have to lead the people here.

"I'm a leader of men and women at this club and and no one wants a leader who talks about his future, about himself, or whatever. And this also not my style."

#809. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

Newcastle United's owners PIF are seeking fresh investment to help the club achieve its infrastructure goals

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At first glance, headlines stating that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has put 25 per cent of Newcastle United up for sale were always going to draw intrigue and perhaps even alarm on Tyneside.

Five years on from the much-heralded takeover that ended Mike Ashley’s unpopular regime, any suggestion of the club’s sovereign wealth owners cashing in naturally invites fears that the project is running out of steam.

However, this proposed transaction is actually one of the more encouraging developments for Newcastle supporters in months.

First and foremost, PIF are not packing their bags and walking away from St James’ Park.

Rather than offloading existing shares to pocket a profit, the club is issuing brand-new equity - with US investment bank J.P. Morgan appointed to find an external partner.

This means not a single penny from the sale will flow back into PIF’s coffers - they are not recouping on their investment. Instead, funds raised through the share issue will supposedly be injected into Newcastle's ongoing projects.

PIF will see its majority stake diluted rather than exiting the club, remaining firmly in the driving seat as owners with majority control.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While fans have grown increasingly frustrated by delays around major infrastructure upgrades, the club, led on the executive side by chief executive David Hopkinson, remains engaged in long-term plans to either substantially redevelop St James’ Park or build a brand-new stadium altogether, alongside the construction of a state-of-the-art training complex.

Bringing in additional investment allows Newcastle to raise hundreds of millions in fresh equity to accelerate those builds, sharing the heavy financial lifting.

After a difficult summer that saw stars like Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon depart to help balance the books, developing Newcastle’s infrastructure and off-pitch revenue streams is the only sustainable way to compete with Europe's elite.

Since original consortium member Amanda Staveley sold her shares and left the board in 2024, ownership of the Magpies has been split between just two parties: PIF holds an 84 per cent majority stake, while the London-based Reuben family - represented on the board by Jamie Reuben, via RB Sports & Media - owns the remaining 16 per cent.

Issuing new shares to cover a 25 per cent stake will dilute both PIF and potentially the Reubens proportionally, leaving PIF with comfortably over 60 per cent of the club and still overall control.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.
