#806. COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment."

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

#805. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

The more things change, the more they stay the same - Watford is an unmanageable club

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no plan, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

However, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

The Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

After Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

Then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

In short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard look at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

In a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or plan - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

Bradley is a sports journalist and Watford fan, who previously spent seven years working for talkSPORT. During his time with the station, he covered the Premier League, EFL and WSL, as well as the Lionesses, and interviewed the likes of Pep Guardiola, Ange Postecoglou, Mikel Arteta, Sarina Wiegman, Alessia Russo, Hannah Hampton and Oscar among others. In his spare time, he is the commentator for Non League side Harefield United. Previously, he worked for Newsquest, covering both Watford and Leyton Orient for the Watford Observer and East London Guardian Series newspapers. He has also had pieces published in the Daily Mail and Watford's matchday programme.

#802. 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."

In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."

The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

With Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."

Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

What is the aim for Kompany, Kane and Bayern?

#801. Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's Â£75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum Â£92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a Â£40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at Â£51m, with Â£4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets â but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about Â£35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined Â£126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

Vinicius Jr signed a new six-year deal at Real Madrid in August

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at Â£100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at Â£80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for Â£116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to Â£120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for Â£117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their Â£80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.

Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose Â£60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of Â£114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about Â£80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum Â£15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly Â£450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?

#798. Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

This article was originally published in Russian.

#797. Chelsea Q&A: Are Blues in crisis? What next for Fofana after viral interview?

Your questions answered by Sky Sports News' James Savundra on Chelsea's season, with Blues having lost three of last four in Premier League; Wesley Fofana’s unauthorised interview, the absences of Danny Welbeck and Estevao, and January transfer plans all addressed

After Chelsea fell to back-to-back losses with a 4-1 humiliation by Leeds at Stamford Bridge last Saturday, Sky Sports News reporter James Savundra examines the latest developments at Stamford Bridge.

As well as suffering a third defeat in four Premier League games, Chelsea and manager Xabi Alonso also faced the added frustration of defender Wesley Fofana giving an unauthorised interview this week, in which he laughed off his penalty miss in last month's Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool and revealed he had contemplated retiring during his time at Stamford Bridge.

Here, Savundra addresses Fofana's future, Joao Pedro's injury, transfer plans and much more...

Jake: Is Fofana expected to face any disciplinary action for his impromptu interview? Some of the things said in that were unacceptable from a footballer, especially one involved in as much off-the-pitch controversy as him.

James says: Xabi Alonso addressed this at Thursday's press conference. Fofana has apologised following the interview. The matter has been dealt with internally and there are no suggestions that the defender is set to miss any matches.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Whether the club look to punish Fofana with a fine is not known at this stage. Alonso made clear that this will not be repeated. It's completely understandable to emphasise with Chelsea supporters. Fofana simply hasn't justified the £75m that Chelsea paid Leicester City.

Benny: Why is Fofana still being chosen when every single fan watching football can see how poor his form is?

James says: At the moment there is a lack of real alternative options. Xabi Alonso stood behind the Fofana-Colwill axis during Thursday's press conference despite their clear struggles dealing with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brian Brobbey.

Liam Delap will prove a similar physical threat tomorrow [Friday] with an added point to prove. Ultimately, Chelsea trimmed down their squad in the summer in light of no European football. Maxence Lacroix would be starting, possibly ahead of Fofana right now if he was fit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Colwill has found things difficult this season having missed the majority of the last campaign. In hindsight, should Chelsea have sold Trevoh Chalobah? Perhaps it was time for the academy graduate to end his Chelsea chapter but he rarely let the side down.

You could feasibly play Josh Acheampong at centre-back. The youngster has been a shining light this season. Yet he looks comfortable on the right. Do you want to upset something which actually seems to be working. And if Acheampong moves to centre-back, then does Marco Palestra play as a right-back?

The Italian impressed in Serie A as a wing-back but with Chelsea opting largely for a flat back four, is Palestra defensively good enough to fulfil that role. Aaron Anselmino remains an option but hasn't played a minute for the club this season.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso of Wesley Fofana: "We have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate. He has apologised. He knows it wasn't the right moment. The content wasn't right. "We are here to take things seriously and he said it wouldn't be repeated. We know it's something we don't want and they are not going to be repeated."

Mikey: Will Chelsea sell and buy any defenders and strikers in January? I feel we need stronger defenders with a better aerial ability and maybe a more out and out No 9 to challenge Joao Pedro and give us something different.

James says: Chelsea will spend money in January if they believe it will help them achieve their target this season - qualifying for the Champions League. They were pleased with what they did in the summer but accept that the squad still requires investment.

It seems unlikely any defenders will be sold given the lack of current options. A loan move would seem to suit Aaron Anselmino given his lack of options. The winter window is a difficult one. There's a sense that Chelsea could benefit from signing a more experienced centre-back, considering the moves for Emi Martinez, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck in every other area of the pitch in the summer.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The club have shown a willingness to tweak their transfer model and sign players for the here and now, in addition to targeting players for the future. A striker would appear unlikely given the presence of Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck. It will be interesting to watch Emegha's development if given a run of games in the absence of Joao Pedro.

The fact that Xabi Alonso opted for a false nine in three matches prior to Leeds would suggest he believes there are shortcomings in both Emegha and Welbeck's games. It feels more likely that Chelsea will revisit the forward line next summer.

JD: How has Joao Pedro's injury affected how Chelsea has been playing as an overall team, and how has Xabi Alonso had to adapt to it?

James says: The stats are undeniable. Since the start of last season, Chelsea average 1.8 goals per game when Joao Pedro plays, compared to 0.6 when he doesn't. It's quite staggering the difference that the Brazilian seems to make.

Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers look far more potent when they are playing off him. Danny Welbeck initially started in his absence at Brentford. However, he had virtually no impact and appears to have fallen down the pecking order.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Playing Rogers or Pedro Neto as a false-nine has been experimented with but Chelsea have looked blunt without a focal point - though Emmanuel Emegha scored in his first Premier League start which was really encouraging.

Xabi Alonso doesn't tend to give much away but he has described Emegha as being a player with "special" qualities. There's clearly an adaptation period required and Emegha missed a lot of football last season due to injury.

He was also signed prior to Alonso's arrival so it was very much a club signing. Chelsea's season has been derailed by the absence of key players such as Reece James, Joao Pedro and Moises Caicedo.

Alonso needs his big players to step up to ensure they can cope with the casualties - albeit to really key players.

Adam: Why does Alonso not start Welbeck whilst Joao Pedro is injured? Given his experience?

James says: The treatment of Welbeck has been puzzling. He performed really well in the opening two Carabao Cup matches of the season but has featured sparingly since the Brentford defeat.

It was interesting to see how late he was brought on against Tottenham despite Chelsea's need to turn the tide. The 36-year-old (happy birthday today, Danny!) clearly cannot get around the pitch with the same intensity and speed he did when he broke through at Manchester United but that was obvious when he was signed.

Alonso has deflected when asked about Welbeck's lack of minutes but perhaps his inability to press with intensity is one of the main reasons behind him spending more time on the bench than on the pitch.

He's still got a brilliant goalscoring touch - as seen last season at Brighton. He may benefit from more opportunities during a busy December period.

Tim: Should Chelsea be starting Estevao more often? If not, then what should we do with him? Where could we send him on loan if we can't guarantee minutes?

James says: Estevao has only started twice this season - both times at home. He made a huge impact on the pitch and on the supporters when he started in the win against Manchester United. His lack of physical robustness and defensive acumen would appear to be why Xabi Alonso has used him so sparingly.

However, I don't think his lack of minutes is going to be sustainable long-term. There's an argument given Cole Palmer's drop off that Estevao should get an opportunity at No 10. Chelsea see Estevao as one of their "untouchable" players and they would be extremely reluctant to let him leave.

I asked Alonso last month about whether a loan could be an option in January. The Spaniard said that it had not been discussed. Something is going to have to give at some point.

Estevao is still a teenager so has lots of learning and development left. However, he would be a key player for many of the top clubs in Europe.

He needs to find a way to force his way into Alonso's plans. A January departure is very unlikely but conversations will need to take place in the summer if his lack of football continues.

Saying that, if Chelsea do qualify for Europe next season then there should be more opportunities.

Sam: Which manager is in more need of a win on Friday, Oliver Glasner or Alonso?

James says: Both clubs feel like they are in very similar situations right now. Both signing managers to deliver a cultural reboot and sustained success. Yet both have had challenging starts.

I was at Glasner's press conference on Thursday and he spoke about lengthy conversations he had with the club owner earlier this week about January transfers and standards. Forest gave him an extremely lucrative contract and will want to give him as much time as they can.

However, given they have had five managers in the space of a year, it's difficult to predict anything at Forest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chelsea have full confidence in Xabi Alonso but home defeats against Spurs and Leeds have really harmed his approval ratings amongst supporters.

It would feel like a crisis if Chelsea lost three league matches on the bounce, so I would say Alonso needs a win just a little bit more than Glasner.

If Forest can create an atmosphere at the City Ground similar to their win against Manchester City then Chelsea will really be tested. Liam Delap will be desperate to prove a point.

It might get worse before it gets better for Manchester City fans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes. Football history is stippled with cautionary tales of managers who followed an all-time great, only to discover that they were doomed from the very beginning.

Manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so. It is impossible not to wonder if the Etihad Stadium is experiencing its very own version of Manchester United's 2013/14.

For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine. Succeeding a figure who loomed so large over the east side of Manchester was never going to be straightforward. Few, though, expected the drop-off to feel quite so jarring, or quite so familiar.

David Moyes arrived at Old Trafford in 2013 tasked with prolonging Sir Alex Ferguson’s dynasty, meanwhile Maresca was handed a three-year contract this summer to keep Guardiola’s juggernaut in motion. Four months into the job, the steering wheel is juddering uncomfortably.

Man City’s recent results make for grim reading compared to the standards set over the last 10 years. A 3-1 defeat away at Nottingham Forest earlier this month was double-take worthy, before Saturday’s 1-1 home draw with Fulham - rescued only by an Elliot Anderson volley - saw them lose yet more ground in the Premier League title race.

On Tuesday night in the Champions League, Man City needed an 86th-minute Rayan Cherki strike just to salvage a 2-2 draw at home to Napoli, currently eighth in Serie A and 14 points off the pace.

Ahead of Sunday’s trip to league leaders Arsenal, Maresca's men look a shadow of the team that so recently struck fear into the Gunners' title hopes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Predictably, the question of Maresca’s future has already begun to take on more of a 'when rather than if' feel. Reports emerged this week suggesting the Italian is fighting to save his job barely a third of the way into his debut Etihad campaign. Sack talk at Manchester City circulating at all, never mind in November, speaks volumes about how rapidly things have changed.

There are parallels between Man City’s recent slump and Moyes’ 10-month spell across town, too. Like Moyes, Maresca inherited a squad undergoing significant churn after an era of dominance.

To bridge that gap, City made a throng of big summer purchases, bringing in additions such as Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez, Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Much like Moyes’ integration of Marouane Fellaini and Juan Mata into a fading champion side, Maresca’s new-look Man City feels disjointed - caught between Guardiola’s positional automatisms and a new manager’s attempt to stamp his own authority on the dressing room.

That disconnect quickly becomes apparent when the team aren't getting results, breeding doubt among players accustomed to certainty and success. All of which begs the question: was Maresca always doomed to fail?

Following Guardiola was always going to be an exercise in managing impossible expectations while rebuilding in real time. Perhaps the Etihad hierarchy believed their structure would insulate Guardiola’s successor from the same sort of post-Ferguson collapse that swallowed Moyes' efforts - which in hindsight weren't all that bad. Perhaps there is a lesson there for Man City chiefs to heed.

Arsenal have a plethora of options in defence, with one out-of-favour star linked with a departure

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal could lose a first-team defender who has fallen out of favour with manager Mikel Arteta.

The Gunners boast arguably the best backline in Europe at the moment, having conceded the fewest goals in the Premier League this term (just seven), and goalkeeper David Raya has already kept seven clean sheets in 11 fixtures.

Part of Arsenal's strength at the back is in their depth – but that could be seriously impacted with interest in a star who hasn't been getting in the team as much of late.

Following a back injury at the 2026 World Cup to William Saliba, the Gunners moved to bring in quality cover in the shape of England international Ezri Konsa.

Konsa has been an instant hit at the Emirates Stadium, and with Arteta now boasting eight senior players competing for places – Konsa, Saliba, Gabriel and Cristhian Mosquera in the centre, with full-backs Jurrien Timber, Ben White, Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapie all capable in the middle, too – the problem is giving each of them playing time.

Sport Witness have now relayed a report from L’Interista that claims Inter Milan are interested in Mosquera, who started the Gunners' first three games of the season in all competitions but hasn't featured much of late.

The Spaniard filled in for Saliba before the Konsa deal was completed, but went off injured against Aston Villa in the second league game of the campaign, paving the way for Konsa to make his debut.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The 29-year-old has kept his place alongside Gabriel ever since – and despite Saliba returning to fitness and featuring on the bench recently, the former Villa star has remained a mainstay of the team.

This has left Mosquera out in the cold as the fourth-choice, and though the ex-Valencia man can play across the backline, White and Timber have rotated for the right-back slot, while Calafiori and Hincapie have shared left-back, leaving him with very few minutes since the start of the campaign.

Mosquera only signed last summer, but with ESPN reporting the transfer fee to be just £13 million, Arsenal may well consider flipping the 22-year-old for a steep profit, with the report claiming Arsenal want around £30m for his signature.

The champions also have a homegrown talent in the form of Marli Salmon, still just 17 years old but having already impressed both centrally and at right-back.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal have no interest in selling Mosquera in January but could reassess the situation next summer.

Mosquera is worth €40 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal host Manchester City this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

#792. Leclerc denies having 'No 1 clause' in Ferrari contract

Lewis Hamilton, meanwhile, confirms they remain "free to race" after talks following their collision in Las Vegas, for which Leclerc was punished by stewards; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Charles Leclerc has strongly denied suggestions he has a No 1 driver clause in his Ferrari contract.

The Monegasque, who has been with the team since 2019 and signed an extended deal earlier this year, was speaking ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix as both he and Lewis Hamilton faced the media again four days on from their latest clash at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing a collision as he attempted to overtake Hamilton for sixth place in Las Vegas, with the incident also earning him severe criticism from Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur.

The Las Vegas collision came just three weeks after a fierce battle between the team-mates - with Hamilton running first and Leclerc second - on the opening lap in Mexico City cost Ferrari a likely one-two, with clear-the-air discussions required after Red Bull's Max Verstappen won that race.

Vasseur has hitherto played down the need to impose strict, pre-determined rules of engagement on his drivers to avoid future repeats. There had subsequently been speculation that, perhaps, there were contractual reasons on Leclerc's side preventing the team from formally intervening in this way.

But offered the chance on Thursday to address claims about the presence of a so-called 'No 1 driver' clause in his deal, Leclerc said: "I normally never disclose what I have in my contract, but I think this one is an important one to speak about.

"And I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract.

George Russell admits feud with Max Verstappen is 'avoidable' and 'unnecessary' ahead of Qatar Grand Prix

Formula 1: 2026 season to end in Europe if Qatar and Abu Dhabi unable to host final rounds because of Middle East conflict

"It's never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc bore the brunt of Vasseur's post-race criticism last Sunday and, asked if he agreed with the Frenchman that the crash with Hamilton had indeed been "unacceptable", replied: "That it is unacceptable? Of course.

"As a team, we cannot afford to clash between team-mates and I think that is very clear for everyone. For the clash in particular of Las Vegas, as I said, I took responsibility.

"I think there's just tension around, that we just need to dissipate and make sure that we look at more positive days in the future.

"That's all I'm looking for. But yeah, I do agree. It's unacceptable that both Ferrari clash together, of course."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Vasseur had promised further talks with his drivers following the race in Vegas, having insisted the clashes between the pair "cannot continue".

The drivers confirmed on Thursday that talks had taken place, with both the team principal and among themselves, with Hamilton saying they had been "good discussions" and "positive".

Neither driver said they would elaborate on the specifics of what was discussed, with Leclerc stating in the official FIA news conference that he "cannot disclose" what possible "solutions" were agreed to avoid future repeats or whether any restrictions were in place for the season's final two rounds.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton later confirmed they remained free to race each other this weekend in Qatar

"We're still free to race, and I think that's the ultimate goal of being here. We want to race, right?" said Hamilton to Sky Sports F1.

"Of course, we don't want what happened last week to ever happen, so we communicate. Charles and I had a good sit down earlier on and had our chat, and I I think moving forwards we can be fine.

"We literally focus on racing hard and fair, and continue to try and enjoy it. We do enjoy racing together, and we do have a really good relationship.

"It's obviously intense in the background, well on the outside, it seems a lot more intense than it really is inside."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton has previously called for the team to adopt clearer guidelines on how he and Leclerc are able to race each other but, speaking on Thursday, said it was Vasseur's final call to make.

"That's for Fred to decide ultimately," he said. "I made my point clear already about them.

"So yeah, there's not really much more to say on it really. I said my piece before and and my point hasn't really changed."

Leclerc and Hamilton are in their second season as Ferrari team-mates and will at least spend one more year in tandem in 2027, with the potential for more.

Asked if he thought they could move forward in harmony, Hamilton said: "I do. We're going to figure it out.

"We're team-mates at the end of the day and we do always learn from these experiences whilst maybe it doesn't necessarily look like it.

"There will be learnings that we take from this difficult period, and I still believe in everything we're building and working towards in the background.

"I came here with the goal of taking Ferrari back to the top and it has been a massively challenging season but it's so easy to look at the negatives but I like to look at the positives this year."

Ferrari can clinch the runner-up position to world champions Mercedes this weekend in Qatar and Hamilton added: "We are fighting for second in the Constructors' Championship, we have had wins, I think we've had the best car chassis-wise particularly this year and that's down to all the amazing people back at the factory who have worked and brought upgrades. I am so proud of them.

"Did we have the straight-line speed? No. That's something we are working towards for next year. If we are able to galvanise and improve on that section, we're going to be mighty next year in my view.

"I'm just trying to look at the positives, I think everyone seems to be focusing always on the negatives, which is obviously the easiest thing to do in life. But I try to remember the positives, and we've really done some amazing things this year together."

Hamilton added: "I like to think that we are stronger. I think that if everything was just great all the time I don't think you learn anything.

"When you're winning all the time as well, you don't learn a lot through that. You learn really through the hardest times, and these are the definitely very, very challenging times for Fred, for Charles and I, but these are the moments that you really learn and grow closer together, through conversation, communicating and having those sit-downs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc believes his off-track relationship with Hamilton is "really strong" and they now needed to find a workable way forward when racing each other on track.

"We're just really very much focused on trying to find a solution that works," said Leclerc.

"Particularly because I really believe we are in a good momentum and if next year we are to be in a position of fighting for the championship, it's even more so important to find the right solution for both of us to bring Ferrari back to the top.

"At the end of the day, we are two, one in each car, and we need to make sure that things just work out. At the moment, it's not working.

"Then, of course, I can take the blame from one episode and whatever. That doesn't really matter. It's just important that we find a compromise and a solution that works for both."

New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino may well be about to address the dreaded left-back problem that has hampered the club for years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United plan to address their issues at left-back by signing a player dubbed ‘the next Riccardo Calafiori’, following another poor result away at Sporting.

The Red Devils dropped two points in Europe last night away in Lisbon, with new manager Mauricio Pochettino winless in his first two games in charge, as the scale of the task at hand becomes clear.

With Manchester United 19th in both the Premier League and the Champions League's league phase right now, Pochettino is under pressure to deliver quickly, with January earmarked for much-needed new signings.

Once again, United have struggled at left-back this season, with veteran Luke Shaw injured for much of the campaign.

Lisandro Martinez started the 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in Pochettino's first fixture, while Diogo Dalot has played out of position to cover there this term, with no obvious candidate to step in during Shaw's absence.

Sport Witness, however, have relayed a report from Gazzetta dello Sport, which claims that United have “already made moves” to sign Juan Miranda of Bologna.

The Spaniard signed for I Rossoblu following the sale of Riccardo Calafiori to Arsenal, and has impressed in Serie A with similar attacking instincts and reliable performances in manager Raffaele Palladino's backline.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While Bologna are looking to tie Miranda down until 2030, there is significant interest from both Pochettino and Newcastle United, who see the 26-year-old as an option to alleviate the burden on Lewis Hall at left-back.

FourFourTwo understands that the Red Devils have a modest budget for January and may be limited in what they can do in the transfer market – meaning that cost-effective signings like Miranda may be the way forward, should Pochettino wish to strengthen.

After finishing third in the Premier League last season, manager Michael Carrick welcomed four new faces to Carrington in the form of Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans – all midfielders – and backup goalkeeper Karl Darlow, along with the returning Marcus Rashford, following his successful stint on loan with Barcelona.

While the lack of depth in defence and attack has been obvious this season though, United's midfield acquisitions have been questioned too for their lack of dynamism, with Carrick ultimately paying for the side's atrocious form with his job after just 10 league games.

United have won just three matches all season in all competitions.

Miranda is worth €15 million, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester United face Brentford this weekend when Premier League action resumes.
